# The First Dream Is Never the Real Dream (how I learned to get unstuck, and you can too)

**Source:** LinkedIn article, 23 March 2025
**Byline at time of writing:** Building things | MD Candidate @ UConn |
Founder @ Rounds | essays on blog.thisisalimirza.com | ex-Epic | views my own

*Pasted by the author. This environment could not reach LinkedIn directly.*

---

When I got into medical school, I felt something I wasn't expecting: lost.

It's not that I didn't want to be there—I did. Since I was a kid, medicine had been the dream. I didn't choose it after weighing my options. I just always knew: I liked science, I liked helping people, and in every story I knew, the doctor was the one who showed up when it mattered.

So I followed that plan. For most of my life, it was all I thought about.

But something strange happens when you finally reach the thing you've been chasing your whole life. You arrive. You pause. And then you ask: now what?

People don't talk about that part. They celebrate the acceptance letter, the white coat ceremony, the goal achieved. But what happens when the dream comes true… and you don't feel complete?

To understand why that moment felt so strange, I have to rewind.

During COVID, I had my first real shift from consumption to creation. I had time. I started reading history and philosophy—Cicero, Galen, Aurelius—and it clicked: these weren't superheroes. They were just people. People who decided to start contributing before they were ready.

That's when I started writing online. I launched thisisalimirza.com to organize my thoughts. It was the beginning of seeing myself as a participant in the world, not just a student of it.

At the same time, I was still laser-focused on med school.

In college, I built what friends know as my "50-year plan":
Become a doctor → build patient trust → influence policy → go into politics → enter pharma → build capital → fund schools and hospitals → return to medicine without the system limitations.

Looking back, it was the kind of ambitious, hyper-structured plan only an analytical college student could write. It assumed the world was a puzzle, and if I played every move right over decades, I could "earn" the right to fix things.

Then I graduated and joined Epic, a large healthcare software company. The job was fine. Stable. Respected. But the day-to-day? Frustrating.

Projects that should take a day took weeks. Meetings about meetings. Decisions slowed by inertia. The only real value I found was watching how company-wide culture was shaped. But the actual work? It felt like mastering someone else's system.

That's when I left. I resigned to pursue med school. But more importantly, I took that year to bet on myself.

That post-Epic year changed me more than anything else.

It taught me I didn't need to wait 50 years. I didn't need permission to start solving problems. I could start now.

That realization completely rewired my mindset.

I stopped thinking in decades-long ladders and started building immediately. I learned to ship, test, iterate. I stopped waiting for the "right time" to contribute and started treating problems as prototypes, not hypotheticals.

What really marked me was a conversation with a serial Entrepreneur from California I reached out to simply because I was pleased to see how often he gave his team kudos in every post he made. Over that conversation he single-handedly inspired me to see who I was denying myself from becoming.

I spent the following months processing that conversation. I was still building JANUS, while also working on learning to code. He bought me a book that he said helped him a lot, and I began reading it every morning between sets at the gym.

There was a slow metamorphosis happening within me and I became hyper-focused on tech and entrepreneurship. I scrapped the whole 50-year plan. I was on trajectory to bypass like 40 years worth of it if I just stayed focused on what was working already.

Then med school started. And for a moment, I felt the tension between the two lives I had lived.

But now, eight months in, I'm more grateful than ever for that year in between. Because I didn't enter med school passively. I came in with momentum.

I've been building ever since. In these 8 months:

- A basic RVU lookup tool: thisisalimirza.github.io/rvulookup/ (Next: auto-suggest optimized codes from physician notes.)
- A patient health literacy screener: careguided.com (Next: use AI to generate personalized education based on the result.)
- A productivity tool for managing multiple priorities. (Next: tailor it to physician workflows.)
- A suicide risk prediction model. (Next: expand to readmission and length-of-stay predictions.)
- A seating management app piloted with 400+ users: usesitr.com (Next: adapt it for hospital bed and room logistics.)

And this is just the beginning.

The first dream is never the real dream. It's just the one that gets you moving.

What I thought would take 50 years, I'm doing piece by piece, now, in my own way. Not because I'm ready. But because I stopped waiting to be.

If you're stuck, take a moment to realize, the only way forward is forward. You won't die by doing the thing. But you might die before you ever get to.
